hero.title: Sources of the Indian Constitution
hero.description: Master the structural core, democratic borrowings, and global inspirations of the Indian Constitution (UPSC GS Paper-2: Polity & Constitution).

timeline.title: Historical Evolution & Milestones
timeline.description: Chronological development leading to the sourcing and enactment of the Constitution.

cards.details: First major attempt by Indians to draft a constitution. It proposed a federal system, bicameral legislature, and a list of fundamental rights, laying the baseline for future borrowings.
Enacted by the British Parliament. It acted as the primary structural source of the Indian Constitution, providing the federal scheme, office of governor, and public service commissions.
The Drafting Committee, chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, scrutinized over 60 global constitutions to borrow and adapt key features to Indian conditions, culminating in adoption on November 26, 1949.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Use these mental hooks to memorize key constitutional borrowings for UPSC Prelims.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: British Borrowings
items.decryption: Remember UK borrowings: **Parliamentary** government, **Writs** (prerogative writs), **Bi**-cameralism, **Cabinet** system, **Single** citizenship (represented by 'In' as Single Unit), and **Law**making/Rule of Law.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: US Borrowings
items.decryption: Remember US borrowings: **President** (Impeachment), **Fundamental** Rights, **Judges** (removal of SC/HC judges), Judicial Review (represented by **Judges**), and **Independent** Judiciary.

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Irish Borrowings
items.decryption: Remember Irish borrowings: **DPSPs** (Directive Principles), **Nominate** (nomination of Rajya Sabha members), and **President** (method of election of the President).

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Test your retention of sources and provisions before diving into tests.

items.question: Which source contributed to about two-thirds of the structural provisions of the Indian Constitution?
items.answer: The Government of India Act 1935. It provided the administrative layout, federal scheme, office of governor, judiciary, and emergency framework.

items.question: What is the crucial difference between Irish and South African Rajya Sabha provisions?
items.answer: Members of Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President from Ireland, whereas they are elected by proportional representation from South Africa.

items.question: Which country inspired the phrase 'Procedure Established by Law' in Article 21, and how does it contrast with the US?
items.answer: Japan. It gives supremacy to the legislature (as long as procedure is followed), whereas the US uses 'Due Process of Law' giving wider review powers to the judiciary.

items.question: Where is the Concurrent List borrowed from, and where is the Joint Sitting of Parliament borrowed from?
items.answer: Both features are borrowed from the Australian Constitution, which also inspired provisions for free trade and commerce.

items.question: Which constitution inspired the suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency, and is it the source of Emergency provisions themselves?
items.answer: The Weimar Constitution of Germany inspired the suspension of FRs. The Emergency provisions themselves are sourced from the GOI Act 1935.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Common Traps
items: Trap 1: Confusing the source of Emergency Provisions (GOI Act 1935) with the source of Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency (Weimar Constitution of Germany).
Trap 2: Confusing Rajya Sabha nominations by the President (Irish Constitution) with the election procedure of Rajya Sabha members (South African Constitution).
Trap 3: Equating Japanese 'Procedure Established by Law' (Article 21) with American 'Due Process of Law'. The former limits judicial review, whereas the latter expands it.

Trap 4: Assuming federalism in India is identical to the US model. The Indian federal system (strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, Governor appointments) is closely modeled on the Canadian Constitution, not the US.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Explore the multi-layered origins of the Indian Constitutional framework.

sections.title: 1. The Government of India Act 1935 (The Structural Backbone)
sections.content:
The Government of India Act 1935 served as the principal structural blueprint for the Indian Constitution, contributing nearly 250 of its articles.

Structural Features Borrowed
  • Federal Scheme: Division of power into Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent lists (though modified post-independence).
  • Office of Governor: The role of Governor as the executive head of the state (though appointment mechanism was later inspired by Canada).
  • Judiciary: The establishment of a unified federal judicial structure, leading directly to the modern Supreme Court and High Courts.
Administrative and Emergency Machinery
  • Public Service Commissions: Provisions for Union (UPSC) and State (SPSC) Public Service Commissions.
  • Emergency Provisions: Under sections 102 and 93 of the 1935 Act, the colonial state exercised emergency powers, which were adapted into Articles 352, 356, and 360 of the Indian Constitution.
  • Administrative Details: Elaborate rules and regulations regarding the daily functioning of executive organs, preventing constitutional vacuum.

sections.title: 2. British & American Influences (System of Governance & Rights)
sections.content:
The institutional design and fundamental rights framework of the Indian Constitution were profoundly shaped by British parliamentary heritage and American constitutionalism.

British Constitutional Borrowings
  • Parliamentary Governance: Prime Minister executive model, responsible Council of Ministers, and Bicameralism (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha).
  • Rule of Law & Writs: Constitutional supremacy over arbitrary power (Article 14) and prerogative writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, etc.) under Articles 32 and 226.
  • Legislative & Cabinet Systems: Single citizenship, cabinet system of governance, parliamentary privileges, and lawmaking procedures.
US Constitutional Borrowings
  • Fundamental Rights: Part III of the Constitution, heavily inspired by the American Bill of Rights.
  • Judicial Independence & Review: Separation of the judiciary from executive control, and the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional.
  • Executive Impeachment & Removal: Impeachment procedure of the President (Article 61) and removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
  • Vice-Presidency: The post of Vice-President as the ex-officio chairman of the Upper House.

sections.title: 3. Sourcing from Canada, Australia, Ireland & Other Nations
sections.content:
To establish a balanced federal system and incorporate welfare ideals, the Constituent Assembly gathered inputs from Ireland, Canada, Australia, and other global democracies.

Canadian & Australian Federations
  • Canada: Federation with a very strong Centre, vesting of residuary powers in the Centre (Article 248), appointment of State Governors by the Centre, and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Article 143).
  • Australia: Concurrent List (Seventh Schedule), freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, and the provision for a Joint Sitting of both Houses of Parliament (Article 108).
Welfare and Rights Inspirations
  • Ireland: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV), nomination of 12 members to the Rajya Sabha, and the electoral college method of electing the President.
  • USSR (Soviet Union): Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and the ideals of Justice (Social, Economic, and Political) in the Preamble.
  • France: The republican form of government, and the ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity in the Preamble.
  • South Africa: The amendment procedure of the Constitution (Article 368) and the election of members of the Rajya Sabha.
  • Germany & Japan: Germany's Weimar Constitution inspired the suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency. Japan contributed the phrase 'Procedure Established by Law' in Article 21.
